newsitem.title: USA: Branch Davidians suffer setback in Waco siege case.
newsitem.headline: Branch Davidians suffer setback in Waco siege case.

text.p: Relatives of 82 Branch Davidian cult members who died in a 1993 siege by federal agents suffered a setback in their bid to sue the government when an appeals court Monday refused to change the judge in the case.
A three-judge panel of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans denied the Branch Davidians' request that U.S. District Judge Walter Smith be removed from the civil case.
Smith presided at a 1994 criminal trial of 11 Branch Davidians in Waco, Texas, and lawyers for the group claim he is biased and incapable of giving them a fair hearing.
"We are pretty certain that if he is our judge we are dead. That's about how bad it is," Mike Caddell, lead counsel for the Banch Davidians, told Reuters Tuesday.

Caddell and other attorneys representing the Branch Davidians, including former U.S. Attorney General Ramsey Clark, alleged the government was trying to cover up evidence that showed federal agents used excessive force in the siege and were to blame for the deaths of 82 Branch Davidians.

The siege began when six cult members and four Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms agents were killed in a shootout at the Branch Davidians' Waco compound as agents moved in to arrest cult leader David Koresh on weapons charges.
It came to a bloody end 51 days later on April 19, 1993, when agents stormed the building and a huge fire then swept through it, killing Koresh and 75 of his followers.

The government says the Branch Davidians themselves set fire to the compound, but survivors and relatives of those killed claim federal agents opened fire on the building and that the fire began when tear gas canisters ignited.

Caddell said lawyers representing the Branch Davidians would ask the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to reconsider their petition for Smith's removal and would go to the U.S. Supreme Court if their request is again denied.

The estates of those killed and more than 200 family members were represented in the civil case. They were looking for hundreds of millions of dollars in damages but it would be a non-jury case so the judge would decide whether or not the government used excessive force and set a figure on damages.

The Waco siege became a rallying cry for anti-government groups and prosecutors alleged that Timothy McVeigh blew up the federal building in Oklahoma City on the second anniversary of the Branch Davidian fire in an act of revenge aimed at sparking an armed uprising against the government.
McVeigh last week was found guilty of the Oklahoma City bombing, which killed 168 people, and a Denver jury was expected to decide this week whether he should be sentenced to death or life in prison.
